title: Food is being used as low-stigma social infrastructure linking affordability, culture, public space, and belonging
source_unit: OECD, Promoting Social Connectedness Through Food
geography: OECD policy context with eight in-depth community-led and government-supported case studies across the United States, United Kingdom, Netherlands, New Zealand, Colombia, Australia, Germany, and Japan, plus examples from other OECD countries

denominator.unit: in-depth food-based case studies selected for the report

policy_shift.value: social connectedness and loneliness are moving onto national and sub-national public-health and social-policy agendas

food_entry_point.value: growing, accessing, preparing, eating, and redistributing food provide purposeful, socially acceptable ways to engage without explicitly framing participation as treatment for loneliness

target_access.value: food-based activities can be adapted across age, income, culture, and ability, including for older and socioeconomically disadvantaged people

cross_outcomes.value: reported potential extends to nutrition, food security, physical activity, mental well-being, skills, employment, urban greening, biodiversity, and climate resilience

observations.method: OECD conceptual synthesis and eight case studies drawn from community-led and government-supported food initiatives; evidence includes interviews and qualitative or participant-reported information.
observations.uncertainty: The report explicitly notes that existing evidence is often qualitative or survey-based and calls for stronger evaluation of magnitude, duration, cost-effectiveness, and subgroup differences.
observations.subgroup: Older people, low-income and unemployed people, people living alone, men experiencing loneliness, migrants and culturally diverse communities, children, volunteers, and residents of under-served neighborhoods.
observations.counterinterpretation: Food can create an accessible reason to meet, but it cannot substitute for income security, safe housing, transport, healthcare, or durable public investment in social infrastructure.

observations.period: 2022; OECD social-connection baseline cited in the 2026 report

denominator.unit: OECD cross-country population baseline from the 2025 Social Connections and Loneliness report

no_support.unit: percent reporting no one to count on in times of need

frequent_loneliness.unit: percent feeling lonely most or all of the time over the previous four weeks

risk_gradient.value: unemployment, low income, lower education, older age, and living alone are associated with poorer social-connection outcomes

observations.method: Secondary use of OECD social-connection indicators to establish the policy problem that food-based initiatives are intended to address.
observations.uncertainty: These are reported association and self-report measures, not evidence that food programmes cause connection or that the same groups benefit equally from them.
observations.subgroup: People with low income, unemployment, lower education, older age, or solo living, as well as men and young people identified as emerging vulnerable groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: Social isolation is multidimensional; frequency of contact, perceived support, relationship quality, and loneliness do not measure the same experience.

observations.period: 2026; food access, shared meals, and daily time patterns

denominator.unit: OECD countries represented in the report's student meal-skipping comparison

meal_skipping.value: at least 1 in 10 students report skipping a meal weekly for financial reasons in each of eight OECD countries shown

shared_family_meals.value: under half of young people in 25 OECD countries have a daily shared family meal

income_gradient.value: food insecurity is most acute among unemployed people and those with lower income or education, while healthy food consumption rises with income

solo_dining.value: United States time-use evidence is presented as showing solo dining on the rise

observations.method: Synthesis of food-security, student, time-use, and shared-meal indicators used to connect material access with social connection.
observations.uncertainty: The indicators come from different sources, years, and countries; meal sharing is not automatically positive, and shared meals cannot be treated as a universal proxy for belonging.
observations.subgroup: Students and young people, low-income households, unemployed people, people with lower education, solo-living adults, and households with constrained food or time budgets.
observations.counterinterpretation: Shared meals may reflect prior household resources and relationships rather than create them; food affordability, schedule control, safety, and cultural fit condition who can participate.

observations.period: 2026; case-study implementation and local social infrastructure

denominator.unit: selected case studies spanning community and government food initiatives

space_reuse.value: vacant urban lots, idle farmland, and under-used community venues are repurposed as gardens, cafés, dining spaces, or cooking venues

government_role.value: public bodies support initiatives through funding, access to land or space, policy alignment, referral pathways, standards, and monitoring

volunteer_dependence.value: many initiatives rely on volunteers, creating both participation and skills benefits but also turnover and burnout risks

service_bridge.value: food activities can draw people into community settings where they later connect with social or support services

cultural_meaning.value: food can enable intercultural exchange and belonging by carrying cultural meaning into shared activities

observations.method: Cross-case implementation synthesis using interviews with programme representatives and analysis of community-led and government-supported initiatives.
observations.uncertainty: Case selection illustrates mechanisms and design challenges but does not estimate population reach, comparative effectiveness, persistence, or cost-effectiveness.
observations.subgroup: Neighborhood residents, volunteers, programme beneficiaries, migrants, culturally diverse groups, children, older adults, local governments, community organizations, and service providers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Volunteer-led food infrastructure can build agency and connection while also shifting unpaid labor and operational risk onto communities, especially where public funding is short-term.

related_sources.claim: Official 92-page OECD report PDF with conceptual framing, food-system stages, eight case studies, and implementation lessons.
Official OECD DOI and publication citation.

boundary: This record adds a food-access-to-social-infrastructure route. It is not a causal evaluation of shared meals, a representative consumer survey, a measure of household food consumption, or proof that food-based initiatives can replace income support, housing, healthcare, or durable public social infrastructure.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official OECD publication page and 92-page report PDF were reviewed for the eight case studies, OECD social-connection baseline, meal-skipping and shared-meal indicators, space-reuse, volunteer, government-support, cultural, and evidence-quality claims.
